final_proof:
The argument as written is not correct. Adding two equations preserves a consequence of the system, but not generally the system itself. For example, over Q, (x = 0 and x = 1) implies 2x = 1, whereas x = 1/2 satisfies the latter equation and not the former system. Thus the induction step needs more than addition.

Here is a precise standard version of the equality statement. Let (K, δ) be a differential field, let R = K[D; δ] be the ring of ordinary linear differential operators, with Da = aD + δ(a), and let R act on a left R-module M. Given L₁,…,Lₙ in R and f₁,…,fₙ in M, there are operators d, Uᵢ, Aᵢ in R such that d = Σᵢ UᵢLᵢ and Lᵢ = Aᵢd for every i. Indeed, R has the right Euclidean algorithm: division by a nonzero operator cancels leading terms because its leading coefficient is invertible. The Euclidean algorithm therefore produces a greatest common right divisor d of the Lᵢ, a Bezout identity d = Σᵢ UᵢLᵢ, and factorizations Lᵢ = Aᵢd. If all Lᵢ are zero, take d, Uᵢ, and Aᵢ all to be zero.

Put h = Σᵢ Uᵢfᵢ. Then

    ∧ᵢ(Lᵢx = fᵢ)  ⇔  (dx = h) ∧ ∧ᵢ(fᵢ = Aᵢh).                 (1)

The second conjunction contains no x. To prove (1), first suppose that all the original equations hold. The Bezout identity gives dx = Σᵢ Uᵢ(Lᵢx) = Σᵢ Uᵢfᵢ = h. Consequently fᵢ = Lᵢx = Aᵢ(dx) = Aᵢh for every i. Conversely, if the right-hand side of (1) holds, then Lᵢx = Aᵢ(dx) = Aᵢh = fᵢ for every i, so all the original equations hold. If all Lᵢ are zero, (1) reads 0 = 0 together with all the necessary and sufficient conditions fᵢ = 0. This proves the corrected equality claim and displays precisely the x-free consistency conditions discarded by the proposed addition step.

The analogous assertion for linear inequations is false, even under these hypotheses. Take K = Q with zero derivation and M = Q, with D acting as zero. Consider x ≠ 0 and x ≠ 1. If L = Σ from j=0 to m of aⱼDʲ, then Lx = a₀x on M. Hence the solution set of a single linear inequation Lx ≠ g is either all of Q, empty, or Q with one point removed: when a₀ = 0 the predicate is constant, and when a₀ ≠ 0 it fails exactly at x = g/a₀. A formula ψ containing no x has one fixed truth value in this structure, so (Lx ≠ g) and ψ still has one of those three kinds of solution set. But the solution set of x ≠ 0 and x ≠ 1 is Q minus {0,1}, which is none of them. Thus no representation of the asserted linear form exists.

There is a correct nonlinear replacement. Over any differential field,

    ∧ᵢ(Lᵢx ≠ gᵢ)  ⇔  ∏ᵢ(Lᵢx − gᵢ) ≠ 0.                         (2)

This is because a field has no zero divisors: a finite product is nonzero exactly when each factor is nonzero. Thus a finite conjunction can be replaced by one differential-polynomial inequation, but generally not by one linear differential inequation.

Finally, writing Lx ≠ g as Lx = g + a with a ≠ 0 requires a new existentially quantified witness a; it is not an equality involving a previously fixed nonzero element. Two such nonzero witnesses can sum to zero. Requiring them to be positive is unavailable over an arbitrary differential field and is not equivalent to allowing arbitrary nonzero residuals. Hence that proposal does not repair the induction.
